text: A pilgrimage costs a fixed sum; selling perfume brings in small change. Abu and his wife mean to make up the difference honestly, which turns much of the film into bookkeeping - a day's takings, a household's needs, a gap that will not close on its own. Salim Ahamed keeps to 104 minutes and stays close to the ground: a house, the road into town, the neighbours who buy and sell alongside them. India's national jury called it the year's best feature, a strange verdict on a picture with so little incident until the refusals start registering. Each shortcut Abu declines has a price attached, and the film troubles to show it. Devotion here is not a mood or a swell of music. It is an amount, assembled coin by coin, by two people who cannot borrow their way to it.

Everything in the frame is plainly false - painted backdrops, staging that makes no attempt at a real place - and the falseness is the argument. Hans-Jürgen Syberberg puts a nineteenth-century German king inside that apparatus, with Wagnerian music underneath and satirical jumps in time cutting across the period whenever he wants them. The proposition is that the national past cannot be filmed as somewhere a person might visit; it can only be mounted, quoted, and taken apart. Figures and traditions arrive already wrapped in their mythology, and the unwrapping is performed by the Germany of 1972 on the Germany it inherited. 135 minutes, with no relief from the artifice at any point. What sounds like a lecture is closer to a seance held in a theatre nobody has cleaned.

152 minutes in 1952, and nothing in them is larger than a household deciding what it can still afford to give away. Shyam is a boy and his mother is teaching him how to behave, and the teaching is never abstract, because the family is poor and every principle gets tested against an actual shortage. Āchārya Atre lets the whole household in - the frictions of people sharing rooms, the obligations that come with relatives, the small humiliations a child registers and does not forget. The national award for best feature went to this, which for material so domestic means a jury was persuaded by conduct rather than event. What holds it together is the mother's voice, applied steadily to a son who will be carrying it long after the lessons stop.

A temple has been left to fall down, and one man still turns up to serve it. He is the Velichappadu, and his function exists only as long as the building and its worship do, so the neglect around him is a verdict the place has delivered without ever saying it aloud. M T Vasudevan Nair sets that against ordinary need: the priest takes leave, a young man steps into the vacant work, and a relationship begins with the Velichappadu's daughter that the older man's position makes impossible to hold at a distance. 128 minutes in Malayalam, most of it in and around one compound. The film's interest is in what becomes of a man whose occupation is belief, at the moment the belief thins out - because it was also a living, and a family ate from it.

A novelist who has turned down prizes everywhere else accepts one from the town he grew up in. Every book Mantovani wrote came out of that place, which means the people preparing his welcome have spent years reading versions of themselves, written by a man who left and did well. Mariano Cohn plays the first stretch as civic comedy - the reception, the ceremony, the interviews - and then lets the discomfort accumulate through hospitality rather than confrontation. The manners are the mechanism. 118 minutes, in Spanish, and the pressure on him is entirely social: a man who converted his neighbours into material has to sit at a table with them and be gracious about it, meal after meal, for as long as the visit lasts.

In 1952 an American production put a peasant revolution into the shape of a western: horses, ridgelines, rifles, a man riding into a village where people are waiting. The revolution is Emiliano Zapata's, against the dictatorship of Porfirio Díaz, and the strain between subject and form is what makes the picture worth an argument - a genre built around one man's competence, handed a mass movement over land. Elia Kazan works in black and white, and the Academy gave that work its art direction award; the look earns it, in adobe and dust and the interiors where officials sit at desks while the country outside changes hands. 113 minutes, and the strain never resolves. The genre keeps offering a hero on horseback; the subject keeps insisting on the thousands behind him.

A hearing aid breaks days before the exams it was needed for, and replacing it becomes a family's entire project. Karim raises ostriches in a dry village; the errand puts him on a motorbike into Tehran, where the day is chopped into paid tasks and a man can earn by carrying other people's things. Majid Majidi runs the two economies against each other for 96 minutes. At home Karim gives instructions and is obeyed. In the city he is one more figure in a queue, and the small opportunities that open there are genuinely tempting, which is exactly what makes them a problem. A Silver Bear went to the lead performance. What accumulates is not incident but objects, favours, and the slow drift in a man's sense of what he is entitled to take.

A doctor pays a soldier to eat nothing but peas and writes down what it does to him. This is one of the odd jobs Franz Woyzeck takes on to put a little more money in front of Marie and their child, and like the others it comes from someone who outranks him and has found a use for him. Werner Herzog takes 82 minutes, short for a tragedy and deliberately so; the humiliations land close together, with no interval in which a man might get his balance back. Marie, meanwhile, has taken up with the drum major, and the town is small. What holds the film in place is how orderly everything is except Woyzeck - the experiment proceeds, the ranks hold, the errands get done, and the only thing coming apart is the man being paid to eat peas.

In this business everyone either casts people or wants to be cast, and every conversation carries a second purpose. Anthony Drazan spends 122 minutes with a small group circling the same rooms and the same grievances - men who describe their own lives with great fluency and get no grip on them whatever. The film is built out of talk rather than incident: long scenes, unbroken argument, performers handed the floor and left standing on it. That is a risk taken knowingly. The comedy comes from how well these people speak; the drama comes from the fact that speaking well changes nothing, and that by 1998 the industry had learned to mistake one for the other. A Volpi Cup went to the lead performance.

Harry teaches roomfuls of young salesmen how to be convincing, and he has just forgotten to collect his own children from the train. Driving country roads afterwards, furious, he nearly runs down a man walking in them - Georges, who has left the institution where he lives because everyone else went home to a family and his mother is dead. From there the film belongs to the two of them, unequally free and unequally in need. Jaco Van Dormael gives it 118 minutes and lets Georges set the pace, which is where the comedy is: the professional persuader has no leverage at all on someone with no interest in being persuaded. Belgium keeps the scale small - roads, houses, other people's weekends carrying on in the background.

The house he grew up in, fields around it, a family holiday out of the city. Then his wife tells him she is expecting a child and that the child is not his. Andrey Zvyagintsev takes 158 minutes over what follows and spends most of them in quiet: a man who cannot bring himself to ask the second question, a woman who has said the only thing she intends to say, rooms where the ordinary noise of a household has stopped. The European Film Award went to the cinematography, and the reason sits in the exteriors - weather visible from a long way off, a road through open country, the house photographed as though it were a party to the conversation. Almost nothing is explained aloud. The film trusts distance, and the distance keeps widening.

The robbery is finished before the trouble starts, which is unusual for a heist picture. Max has the gold and what he wants with it is quiet - good meals, clean shirts, an old friend to spend the evenings with - and Jacques Becker gives 95 minutes to the upkeep of that modest ambition. The crime plot is standard issue: a rival wants the stash, Riton is the way to get at it, and the pressure begins with something Max told a woman he should not have told. What is not standard is the attention. Becker films the eating, the undressing, the small courtesies, and treats a friendship between two aging men as the one thing worth risking anything over. The genre asks for nerve. This one is about fatigue, and about what a habit costs to keep.

Release from a psychiatric hospital is not the same thing as being taken back. The man walking out has a wife who is no longer his wife, and an idea that whatever put him inside can be answered for now, in person, at this late date. Nick Cassavetes films that idea at close range for 100 minutes and does not tidy it up. Romance and thriller are both attached to the picture, and the pairing is honest - the feeling is real, so is the alarm it sets off in everyone standing nearby, and the film declines to rank them. What it has in place of a plot is escalation: two or three people in a room, talking well past the point where talking helps, the performances left to carry whatever the writing refuses to settle.

Two half-brothers, raised by a mother whose attention went to her own affairs, came out of that childhood pointed in opposite directions. One went into molecular biology, where genes are more interesting than people; the other into a permanent, unsatisfied pursuit of sex. Oskar Roehler adapts Michel Houellebecq's novel by running both lives alongside each other for 105 minutes, so that each arrangement comments on the other without a word of commentary. Then a woman enters each story - Christiane for Bruno, Annabelle for Michael, who knew her when they were young - and the real question surfaces: whether men assembled this way can be reached by anyone. The humour is dry and unkind. Whatever tenderness the film allows is not offered as a cure.
